In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of stable isotopes to paleoecology, specifically to reconstruct the biogeography and ecology of C3/C4 grasses.
the application of the phytolith technique for reconstructing past grassland ecosystems.

the application of the stable carbon isotope ratios of phytolith (silica bodies formed in the tissues of grasses) to reconstruct changes in the relative contribution of C3 andC4 grasses to Neogene grasslands of North America.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

soil phytolit carbon isotope ratios are useful in distinguishing C4 grasses from C3 plants, but that the degree of isotopic compression and/or depletion is not yet fully understood and requires additional research.
soil phytolit δ13C values are not as depleted as phytoliths directly extracted from plants.
phytolith carbon isotopic signatures are a promising tool for the reconstruction of C3 and/or C4 grassland biogeography.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
soil phytolit δ13C values are a promising proxy for the C3/C3 grass contribution to the vegetation.
the isotopic composition of phytolith δ18O and δ13C can provide information on the relative abundance of C3 and/or C4 grasses in a paleoenvironment.
the δ13C value of phytolith δ18O values are useful proxies for the relative abundance of C3 and/or C4 grasses in the soil.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phytolith asoils provide a record of C3/C4 grass abundance in the past.
phytolith carbon isotopes are an effective tool for quantifying the relative contribution of C3 vs C4 grasses to the soil.
the δ13C of soil phytolitsh is a useful tool for reconstructing C3/C4 grassland dynamics, but the application of this proxy to the Neogene requires the use of empirically derived end-members.
